items.prompt: Which technique decides how many users get a new version first?
choices: Blue-green deployment
Canary deployment
Feature flag
items.explanation: A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first.

items.prompt: Which technique keeps two full environments and moves traffic between them?
choices: Blue-green
Canary
Feature flag
items.explanation: Blue-green runs two complete environments and switches all traffic from one to the other.

items.prompt: Which technique turns a single behavior on or off while the app keeps running?
choices: Blue-green deployment
Feature flag
Canary deployment
items.explanation: A feature flag is a runtime toggle for one piece of code.

items.prompt: In the soup story, what does serving 10 of 200 diners first correspond to?
choices: A second kitchen
A menu toggle
A small first slice
items.explanation: A small first group trying the new thing is the canary idea.

items.prompt: What does blast radius mean?
choices: How long a deploy takes to finish
How many users a bug can reach
How many servers a team looks after
items.explanation: Blast radius is the number of users a mistake can reach.

items.prompt: Why can staging miss some bugs?
choices: Real traffic has patterns staging lacks
Staging servers are always slower
Staging never runs the new code
items.explanation: Real users bring data, habits and scale that a test environment only approximates.

items.prompt: What is blue-green mainly good at?
choices: Limiting which users see a new version
Hiding unfinished code from some users
A fast switch back to a good version
items.explanation: Blue-green's strength is a quick switch back, not limited exposure.

items.prompt: What does progressive delivery mean?
choices: Deploying only outside working hours
Rolling out in stages, checking each
Releasing only to a test environment
items.explanation: Rolling out in stages, with a health check at each stage, is progressive delivery.

items.prompt: A team uses blue-green and ships a bug to 100% of users. Once spotted, switching back takes seconds, but spotting took 15 minutes. What did blue-green cover?
choices: It made going back fast, but did nothing to limit how many users met the bug first
It limited the bug to a small slice, but made going back slow once the bug was found
It kept the bug hidden behind a switch until someone turned it on for those users
It prevented the bug by trying the green environment on real traffic before any switch
items.explanation: Blue-green moves all traffic at once. The 15 minutes were spent at full exposure; only the return trip was fast.
items.reference:
Three techniques, three questions
🥄 canary: how many users try it first?
🔁 blue-green: how fast can we switch back?
🎚️ feature flag: is this one behavior on right now?
Why: each technique answers a different question, so the risk you name decides the tool.
items.learnMore:
Matching the tool to the risk

A canary limits the number of people who meet a bug. Blue-green shortens the time to go back once someone decides to. A flag turns one behavior off without touching the rest. A fast switch back does nothing for the minutes before anyone notices the bug.

Common mistake

Assuming blue-green limits who sees the new version. It moves all traffic at once, so it makes going back fast but exposure total.
items.reflection: Think of a change you once made for everyone at once. Which small group could have tried it first?

items.prompt: One new ranking behavior inside a big release looks risky, the rest is fine, and it must be switchable off in seconds with no new deploy. Which tool matches?
choices: Blue-green, because swapping environments rolls back the whole release as one unit
A feature flag guarding that behavior, so the rest of the release stays live
A 5% canary on the whole release, because it also limits the safe parts
Longer staging tests, because staging can reproduce real traffic patterns
items.explanation: Only a flag isolates a single behavior and flips at runtime. Blue-green and canary act on the whole version.

A config typo that staging already caught and that has no user impact on anyone
items.explanation: The canary's job is limiting how many users meet an unknown, traffic-dependent bug.

choices: Yes: switching whole environments is the same thing as rolling out gradually in stages
No: blue-green is unrelated to rollout safety and it should not be used for releases
Yes, provided the green environment was already tested in staging beforehand by the team
Only partly: staged exposure with health checks is the half that blue-green lacks

items.prompt: What is the first canary stage in this unit?
choices: 50% of traffic
100% of traffic
5% of traffic
items.explanation: The staged model starts small, at 5%.

items.prompt: What happens when a stage is unhealthy?
choices: The rollout skips to 100%
The rollout halts and goes back
The rollout waits and ignores it
items.explanation: An unhealthy check halts the rollout and returns to the previous safe state.

items.prompt: What is an error rate?
choices: Failed requests divided by all requests
Total requests handled each second
Servers in the rollout divided by users
items.explanation: Error rate compares failures with all the traffic they came from.

items.prompt: What is a monitoring window?
choices: The share of users placed in a stage
The list of users who joined the canary
The time spent watching a stage
items.explanation: It is the period of watching before a stage is called healthy or not.

items.prompt: Why start at 5% rather than 50%?
choices: Small slices always run faster
Less exposure while evidence is thin
Large slices always cost more
items.explanation: A small first slice keeps the damage small while you know least.

items.prompt: A stage was healthy at 25%. Is a check at 50% still needed?
choices: Yes, a bigger slice can show new problems
No, 25% proves everything
No, 50% is always safe
items.explanation: Each stage is evidence only about its own slice and load.

items.prompt: What is a threshold?
choices: The number of servers in a stage
The date a rollout ends
The agreed limit that triggers a halt
items.explanation: Crossing the threshold means the stage is unhealthy.

items.prompt: Which of these is a real gate?
choices: A ten-minute wait with no check
A health check that must pass
A meeting on the calendar
items.explanation: A gate can say no; a timer cannot.

items.prompt: A canary was healthy at 25%. What is the strongest reason to still run a fresh check at 50%?
choices: A bigger slice brings more load and more user types, so new problems can appear
The earlier result expires after a fixed number of minutes whatever happens in between
The 25% check only counted crashes and never counted slow requests of any kind at all
A second check lets the team skip the monitoring window at the next stage entirely
items.explanation: A pass at one stage describes that stage's users and load only.
items.reference:
Each stage is a gate
5% → check → 25% → check → 50% → check → 100%
unhealthy at any check: halt and go back
crashes alone miss quiet quality bugs
Why: a stage is evidence about its own slice and load, so each step needs its own check.
items.learnMore:
Why every stage has its own check

A stage that looks healthy tells you about the users and load in that stage. A bigger slice brings more load and a wider mix of users, so a problem can first appear there. The check must also measure something tied to the feature, or quiet bugs pass.

Common mistake

Counting only crashes. A change that returns worse results without failing a single request looks perfectly healthy to that signal.
items.reflection: Think of something you introduced in steps, like a new route to work. What told you it was safe to take the next step?

items.prompt: A recommendation canary shows no crashes, but users click far fewer recommendations. Which statement is right?
choices: The canary worked as designed, since no requests failed, so the rollout should advance
Crash counts missed a quality regression; the gate needs a metric tied to the feature
The stage was too small, since only a 100% rollout can reveal changes in click rates
Click rates cannot be measured on a canary, so they must not be used in any gate
items.explanation: A bug that returns worse results without failing requests is invisible to a crash signal.

choices: A larger first stage, since 5% is too small to learn anything from at all
A second timer so each stage waits twice as long before moving on again
A rollback to 0% after every stage to reset the counts for the next one
A health check that can say no; a timer alone gathers no evidence
items.explanation: A gate must be able to say no. A timer only delays.

items.prompt: What does a deploy change?
choices: Which users see a behavior
Which flags exist
Which code is running
items.explanation: A deploy puts code onto production servers.

items.prompt: What does a release (flag turned on) change?
choices: The server hardware in use
Who sees the behavior
The build tools in use
items.explanation: Turning the flag on decides who experiences the behavior.

items.prompt: A flag is OFF. Do users see the new behavior?
choices: No
Yes, everyone
Yes, half
items.explanation: With the flag off, the old path serves everyone.

items.prompt: What is the fastest way to undo a bad flagged feature?
choices: Redeploy the old build
Rebuild the servers
Turn the flag off
items.explanation: Flipping the flag needs no deploy.

items.prompt: Does flipping a flag need a new deploy?
choices: Yes, always
No, it flips at runtime
Yes, but only at night
items.explanation: Flags are read while the app is running.

items.prompt: What does runtime mean here?
choices: While the app is already running
While the code is compiled
Before the code is written
items.explanation: Runtime is the period when the app is already up.

items.prompt: What is a downside of keeping old flags?
choices: They slow down the network
They delete user data
Extra branches to understand and test
items.explanation: Every leftover flag is another path someone must reason about.

items.prompt: Which risk is not behind a flag?
choices: A new button's behavior when clicked
A migration that runs on deploy
A new menu item shown to users
items.explanation: Deploy-time work runs regardless of any flag.

items.prompt: New checkout code is deployed with its flag OFF, and orders start failing. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The new path is not the cause yet, since users are still on the old path
Turn the flag ON, so the new path replaces the failing one for everyone
Turn the flag OFF, which will certainly stop the failures that began
Redeploy the previous build, because the flag changes nothing about routing
items.explanation: Off means the new code is not serving anyone, so look elsewhere first.
items.reference:
Deploy and release are separate events
deploy: code reaches production (flag OFF)
release: flag ON for a small group, then everyone
problem found: flag OFF, no new deploy
Why: a flag lets you undo a release as fast as flipping a switch, without redeploying.
items.learnMore:
What a flag does and does not guard

Code that ships with its flag off changes nothing for users. Turning the flag on is the release, and turning it off is the rollback. A flag only protects code written behind it, so a database migration or an infrastructure change is outside it.

Common mistake

Believing a flag protects the whole deploy. Anything that runs at deploy time, outside the guarded branch, happens whatever the flag says.
items.reflection: Where in daily life do you put something in place first and switch it on later?

items.prompt: A rollout relies on flags, but a schema migration runs automatically at deploy and locks a table. Why does the flag not help?
choices: Flags only work on front-end code and never on back-end services at all
The migration runs as part of the deploy, outside any code the flag guards
Flags only take effect after midnight, so the daytime migration came first
Flags are checked once a week, so the change was not seen in time to act
items.explanation: A flag guards a code branch, not work done at deploy time.

choices: Switch the flag on in the code, then ship it to every server at once
Ship to a few servers first, then enable the flag for all users at once
Ship with the flag off, enable it for a small group, then widen it
Wait for a quiet hour, then ship and enable in the same single step
items.explanation: Deploy first with the behavior dark; release is the later, gradual step.

choices: The flag silently turns itself off for some users each month at random
The pipeline can no longer ship code that touches the file with the flag
The flag's state is deleted whenever the servers happen to restart
Every future change must reason about a branch that no longer varies
items.explanation: Dead flags add paths to read and test with no benefit.

items.prompt: What does hashing a user id give you?
choices: A new random number each time
The user's password
A fixed bucket from 0 to 99
items.explanation: The same id always hashes to the same bucket.

items.prompt: A user has bucket 3 and the canary is 5%. Which version?
choices: Old
New
Both
items.explanation: 3 is below 5, so the user is in the canary.

items.prompt: A user has bucket 60 and the canary is 25%. Which version?
choices: Old
New
Both
items.explanation: 60 is not below 25, so the user stays on the old version.

items.prompt: Does the same user id always land in the same bucket?
choices: No
Only on weekdays
Yes
items.explanation: That is the point of hashing.

items.prompt: The canary rises from 5% to 25%. Which buckets are added?
choices: 0 through 4
5 through 24
25 through 99
items.explanation: Buckets 0 to 4 were already in; the new range is 5 to 24.

items.prompt: Is a per-user record stored to remember the assignment?
choices: No, the id decides it
Yes, in a users table
Yes, in a cookie per request
items.explanation: The hash is recomputed from the id every time.

items.prompt: Why not flip a coin on each request?
choices: Coins are slow to flip
Coins cannot give exactly 5%
A user would see both versions
items.explanation: Random per-request choice mixes the two versions for one person.

items.prompt: A user has bucket 40 and the canary is 50%. Which version?
choices: Old
New
Neither
items.explanation: 40 is below 50, so the user is in the canary.

items.prompt: user-7 hashes to bucket 77. The rollout goes 25%, then 50%, then 100%. When does user-7 first get the new version?
choices: At the 100% stage
At the 25% stage
At the 50% stage
Never joins the canary
items.explanation: A bucket is in the canary only when it is below the percentage: 77 is below 100 but not below 50.
items.reference:
The same user, the same bucket
user id → hash → bucket 0 to 99
bucket below canary percent: new
raise the percent: only adds buckets
Why: the id decides the bucket, so nobody flips back and nothing is stored.
items.learnMore:
Why hashing beats coin flips

A coin per request gives one person both versions and mixes your measurements. Hashing the id gives a fixed bucket, and the percentage is just a cut-off. Raising the cut-off adds users without moving anyone already included.

Common mistake

Changing the hash function mid-rollout. Buckets change, users flip versions, and the evidence gathered earlier no longer describes the same people.
items.reflection: Where does a fixed rule, like a birth month, put people in the same group every time?

items.prompt: A user has bucket 24. What are their versions at 24% and at 25%?
choices: New at 24%, new at 25%
Old at 24%, new at 25%
Old at 24%, old at 25%
New at 24%, old at 25%
items.explanation: 24 is not below 24, but it is below 25. Buckets join as the cut-off passes them.
items.reference:
The same user, the same bucket
user id → hash → bucket 0 to 99
bucket below canary percent: new
raise the percent: only adds buckets
Why: the id decides the bucket, so nobody flips back and nothing is stored.

items.prompt: Why does raising the percentage never move a user back to the old version?
choices: The system records each user's last version in a table and keeps it forever
Users already on the new version are skipped when the hash is computed again
Buckets are fixed per user, and a higher cut-off only includes more buckets
Rollouts only move in 25-point steps, so reshuffling cannot happen between them
items.explanation: The comparison is bucket against a growing cut-off, and no state is involved.

user id → hash → bucket 0 to 99
bucket below canary percent: new
raise the percent: only adds buckets

items.prompt: Someone swaps the hash function while the rollout sits at 25%. What happens?
choices: Nothing changes, since each user's version is stored per user and survives any change of hash
Every user moves to the new version, since the new hash starts every bucket at zero for all
Only users above bucket 25 are affected, while all the others keep the version they had
Many users' buckets change, so some flip versions and earlier evidence no longer fits them
items.explanation: New hash means new buckets. Stability depends on the hash staying fixed for the whole rollout.

items.prompt: A bug breaks 1% of users. What is the overall canary error rate with a fair sample?
choices: About 5%
About 100%
About 1%
items.explanation: A fair sample holds the same 1% share of affected users.

items.prompt: What is a segment?
choices: A single server in the fleet
A group sharing a trait
A stage of the rollout plan
items.explanation: A segment is a group such as users in one region.

items.prompt: Does a bigger canary raise the overall rate of a 1% segment bug?
choices: No, it stays about the same
Yes, it doubles
Yes, it reaches 100%
items.explanation: The affected share is the same at every canary size.

items.prompt: How can you see a segment bug?
choices: Wait until 100%
Count total requests only
Check the error rate per segment
items.explanation: A per-segment view undoes the dilution.

items.prompt: What does averaging over everyone do to a small group's problem?
choices: It amplifies it
It dilutes it
It deletes the group
items.explanation: A few failures disappear into many successes.

items.prompt: In the example, what is the error rate inside the affected region?
items.explanation: Every user in the region fails, so inside it the rate is total.

items.prompt: Which overall threshold would trip on a 1% overall rate?
items.explanation: A rate trips a threshold only when it is above it.

items.prompt: What does a fair sample mean for a 5% canary?
choices: It holds only brand-new users
It mirrors the full user mix
It holds only the company's own staff
items.explanation: The canary reflects the same mix as everyone.

items.prompt: A bug fails every user in a region that is 1% of all users. The halt threshold is 2% overall. What happens at a 25% canary?
choices: No halt: the overall rate is about 1%, under 2%, though one region fails fully
Halts: 250 failed users out of 25,000 is far above the 2% overall threshold
Halts: a 25% canary always doubles the error rate of any segment bug it meets
No halt, because the affected region is excluded from the canary at 25% size
items.explanation: 250 / 25,000 = 1%, below 2%. The region's own rate is 100%, but the overall rate hides it.
items.reference:
A 1% segment bug, 5% / 25% / 100% canary
overall error rate: about 1% at every size
affected region: 100% errors inside its slice
threshold 2% overall: never halts
Why: a fair sample keeps the same small share of affected users, so a bigger canary does not make the average louder.
items.learnMore:
Averages hide small groups

A canary is a fair sample, so it holds the same share of each group as the whole user base. A group that is 1% of users stays 1% of the canary at any size, and its failures stay diluted in the overall rate. Looking at the rate inside that group is what exposes it.

Common mistake

Assuming a bigger canary will make a rare bug visible. Size adds users but not contrast; only a per-group view adds contrast.
items.reflection: Think of a number that looked fine on average. Which small group might it have hidden?

items.prompt: Which addition would stop this rollout early?
choices: A second overall rate computed over only the last hour
Error rate per region, with its own threshold
A larger canary slice with the same overall threshold
A count of total requests with no error information
items.explanation: Only a per-region view shows the 100% rate inside the affected region.

overall error rate: about 1% at every size
affected region: 100% errors inside its slice
threshold 2% overall: never halts

items.learnMore:
Averages hide small groups

A canary is a fair sample, so it holds the same share of each group as the whole user base. A group that is 1% of users stays 1% of the canary at any size, and its failures stay diluted in the overall rate. Looking at the rate inside that group is what exposes it.

Common mistake

Assuming a bigger canary will make a rare bug visible. Size adds users but not contrast; only a per-group view adds contrast.
items.reflection: Think of a number that looked fine on average. Which small group might it have hidden?

items.prompt: A segment is 2% of users. A 5% canary of 100,000 users holds 5,000 users. About how many segment users are in it?
items.reference:
A 1% segment bug, 5% / 25% / 100% canary
overall error rate: about 1% at every size
affected region: 100% errors inside its slice
threshold 2% overall: never halts
Why: a fair sample keeps the same small share of affected users, so a bigger canary does not make the average louder.

items.prompt: Why does making the canary bigger not fix the blind spot?
choices: A bigger canary leaves out the affected users, which hides them from the monitoring
A bigger canary needs a bigger threshold, which cancels out any gain in detection
Only the first 5% of users are ever monitored, however large the canary becomes
A fair sample keeps the same affected share, so the overall rate barely moves
items.explanation: Size adds users in proportion, so the average does not change.

items.prompt: Implement `errorRate(errors, total)`: the error rate as a percentage. Compute `errors * 100 / total`.
items.explanation: Multiply first and divide last: 50 * 100 / 1000 is exactly 5.

items.prompt: Implement `exceeds(rate, threshold)`: true only when the rate is strictly above the threshold.
items.explanation: Sitting exactly on the threshold is allowed, so the comparison is strict.

items.prompt: Implement `canaryUsers(total, percent)`: how many users a canary of that percent holds, rounded down.
items.explanation: Multiply by the percent, divide by 100, and round down to whole users.

items.prompt: Implement `bucketIsNew(bucket, percent)`: true when a user's bucket (0 to 99) is below the canary percent.
items.explanation: Buckets 0 to percent-1 are in the canary, so the comparison is strictly less than.

items.prompt: Implement `nextStage(current, stages)`: the stage after `current` in the list, or `null` if it is the last.
items.explanation: Find the current position and return the following entry, or null at the end.

items.prompt: Implement `usersOnOld(total, percent)`: how many users stay on the old version (total minus the canary users, rounded down as in a canary).
items.explanation: Count the canary users first, then subtract them from the total.

items.prompt: Implement `enoughTraffic(total, minRequests)`: true when a stage has at least `minRequests` requests to judge from.
items.explanation: Exactly the minimum is enough, so the comparison includes equality.

items.prompt: Implement `stageLabel(percent)`: return "off" for 0, "full" for 100, and "canary" for anything in between.
items.explanation: The two ends are special cases; everything between them is a canary stage.

items.prompt: Implement `shouldHalt(errors, total, thresholdPercent)`. Halt (return `true`) only when the error rate is strictly above the threshold; with no requests at all, do not halt. Avoid dividing: compare `errors * 100` with `thresholdPercent * total`.
items.explanation: The rate is errors/total, so the check compares rates, not counts. Zero traffic gives nothing to judge, and the exact-threshold case (2% vs 2%) does not halt.
items.reference:
Halt on a rate, not a count
20 errors / 1,000 requests = 2% → over a 1% limit
20 errors / 10,000 requests = 0.2% → under it
no requests: nothing to judge, do not halt
Why: the same count means different things at different traffic, so compare a rate to a threshold.
items.learnMore:
The halt rule as a small function

A rate needs both parts, errors and total traffic. Multiplying before dividing avoids float surprises. The two edge cases to name are zero traffic and landing exactly on the threshold.

Common mistake

Dividing by a total of zero, or comparing the raw error count against a fixed number that ignores traffic.
items.reflection: Where have you seen a raw count mislead because the volume behind it was different?

items.prompt: Implement `shouldHaltBySegment(segments, thresholdPercent)`. `segments` is an array of `{ errors, total }`. Return `true` if any segment with traffic has an error rate strictly above the threshold; otherwise `false`.
items.explanation: Each segment is judged on its own rate, so one fully failing small segment halts even when the overall rate is low.

no requests: nothing to judge, do not halt

items.prompt: Implement `canaryAction(errors, total, thresholdPercent, minRequests)`. Return "wait" if `total` is below `minRequests`; otherwise "halt" if the error rate is strictly above the threshold; otherwise "advance". Compare `errors * 100` with `thresholdPercent * total`.
items.explanation: Too little traffic means no verdict yet. With enough traffic the rate decides: above the threshold halts, otherwise the stage advances.

items.prompt: Implement `nextPercent(current, stages, healthy)`. If not healthy, return 0. If healthy, return the next stage after `current` in `stages`, or `current` if it is already the last.
items.explanation: Unhealthy always goes back to 0. Healthy moves one stage forward and stays put at the end.
